concept.concept_description: The Stone-Weierstrass theorem guarantees that any continuous function can be approximated by an algebra that separates points and contains constants. Conjecture: The algebra of EML functions (finite compositions of exp, log, +, *) on any compact subset of R^n is dense in C(K) with a Jackson-type rate: for f in Lip_alpha(K), there exists an EML network of width O(epsilon^{-n/alpha}) approximating f within epsilon. The constants are included via c = exp(a)*log(c) for c > 0. This gives EML networks provable approximation guarantees with explicit rates, going beyond the existential guarantees of universal approximation theorems. Test: prove the separation property (given x != y in K, find EML parameters that separate them) and the rate bound for Lipschitz functions. Construct an EML network of width n approximating x^2 on [0,1] with explicit error bounds. Impact: gives EML networks provable approximation guarantees with explicit rates, surpassing the existential guarantees of universal approximation theorems.

concept.title: Uniform Extremality for Siblings of the Coupon Collector
concept.concept_description: For every fixed N ≥ 2 and j ≥ 2, the expected number of empty spaces E_p[U_j^N] in the j-th sibling's album at the main collector's completion time is uniquely maximized over the open probability simplex by the uniform distribution p = (1/N, ..., 1/N). Moreover, E_p[U_j^N] is Schur-concave in p, so it strictly decreases along every nonconstant ray from the uniform vector within the simplex.
concept.mathematical_framing: For every fixed N ≥ 2 and j ≥ 2, the expected number of empty spaces E_p[U_j^N] in the j-th sibling's album at the main collector's completion time is uniquely maximized over the open probability simplex by the uniform distribution p = (1/N, ..., 1/N). Moreover, E_p[U_j^N] is Schur-concave in p, so it strictly decreases along every nonconstant ray from the uniform vector within the simplex.
concept.lean_guess: Express E_p[U_j^N] via the Adler–Oren–Ross integral formula, then verify the Schur-concavity of the integrand as a function of p using the Schur–Ostrowski criterion (the partial derivative monotonicity condition). Since the uniform distribution majorizes every probability vector on the simplex, Schur-concavity implies it uniquely maximizes the expectation. ## 1. The two ingredients

For a graph `G` with maximum degree `d`, a **signing** `σ` assigns `±1` to each edge and
produces a symmetric signed adjacency matrix `A_σ`. We study `ρ(A_σ) = max |μ|` over the
eigenvalues `μ`.

* **Trace-moment control.** For any symmetric matrix, `tr(A^{2k}) = Σ_i μ_i^{2k} ≥ μ^{2k}`

* **Averaging.** `tr(A_σ^{2k})` is an *additive* functional of the matrix, so the minimum
  over a family of signings is at most the average. The best signing beats the average.

## 2. Why the average kills odd walks (the source of the constant)

`tr(A_σ^{2k}) = Σ_v (number of closed walks of length 2k at v, signed by ∏ σ(edge))`.
Averaging over all `2^{|E|}` signings, a closed walk survives **iff every edge is used an
even number of times** (otherwise its sign averages to 0). Small-case counts of these
"even closed walks" for a `d`-regular graph:

| walk length 2k | all closed walks (≈) | even closed walks bound |

# Future Directions: Signings, Spectral Moments, and the Bilu–Linial Frontier

The results of this cycle separate the existence of a good edge-signing into two clean
halves: an elementary *averaging* principle (the best member of a family beats its
average even spectral moment) and a hard *combinatorial* estimate (how large that average
moment can be). The conjectures below are the natural bold targets that this separation
exposes.

## Conjecture 1 — The even-walk constant is exactly 3(d-1)

For every graph of maximum degree `d`, the average over all edge-signings of the
`2k`-th spectral moment grows like `(3(d-1))^k` times the number of vertices, and this
rate is achieved by trees near a high-degree vertex.

*The key insight is* that averaging over signings annihilates every closed walk that
traverses some edge an odd number of times, leaving only "even" closed walks whose
growth rate is set by the branching factor `3(d-1)` rather than the naive `d^2`.

*Why now?* The averaging half of the argument is now settled unconditionally, so the
entire improved spectral bound `2√(3(d-1))` reduces to this single scalar walk-counting
statement — a self-contained combinatorial problem detached from any spectral technology.

## Conjecture 2 — Unbalance is the deterministic route to sub-degree spectra

Every non-bipartite graph admits an explicit signing, obtained by making a suitable
odd-length cycle unbalanced, whose spectral radius is strictly below the maximum degree;
moreover the amount of improvement is controlled by the girth.

*The key insight is* that an unbalanced cycle forces the shortest closed walks around it
to enter with opposite signs and cancel, deterministically reproducing the cancellation
that the probabilistic method only achieves on average.

*Why now?* The 4-cycle witness shows the mechanism concretely (spectral radius `√2`
against degree `2`); the remaining question is purely which cycles to unbalance, a local
and testable construction.

## Conjecture 3 — Non-backtracking moments reach the Ramanujan constant

Replacing ordinary closed walks by non-backtracking closed walks in the moment method
lowers the achievable constant from `3(d-1)` all the way to the optimal `d-1`, so a
signing exists with spectral radius at most `2√(d-1)` for every `d`-regular graph.

*The key insight is* that the backtracking steps are exactly the walks responsible for
the excess factor of `3`; excising them by working with the non-backtracking operator
should collapse the constant to its conjecturally sharp value.

*Why now?* With the moment-to-existence reduction in hand, the optimal Bilu–Linial bound
becomes equivalent to a clean estimate on non-backtracking walk counts, isolating the one
place where sharper combinatorics is genuinely required.

## Conjecture 4 — Signings compose under graph lifts

If a base graph has a signing with spectral radius `r`, then every `2`-lift of it has a
signing with spectral radius at most `r`, and iterating produces an infinite family of
bounded-degree expanders with a uniform spectral-radius bound.

*The key insight is* that a `2`-lift's spectrum is the union of the base spectrum and the
spectrum of a signed version of the base, so a good signing of the base transfers to the
lift without loss.

*Why now?* This is the exact structure the interlacing-families method exploits; making
the transfer quantitative and unconditional would turn a single good signing into an
entire tower of expanders.

## Conjecture 5 — A moment certificate for spectral gaps

A finite family of symmetric matrices has a member with a prescribed spectral-radius
bound if and only if a single averaged even-moment inequality holds for the family; the
certificate size is polynomial in the matrix dimension.

*The key insight is* that the even spectral moment is simultaneously an upper bound on
each eigenvalue and an additive (hence averageable) functional, so one scalar inequality
encodes an entire existence statement.

*Why now?* The averaging principle proved this cycle already gives the "if" direction in
full; a matching converse would make "there exists a good member" a decidable,
certificate-checkable property, with immediate algorithmic consequences for constructing
low-spectral-radius signings.

concept.title: No-Stretching Property of GF(2) Quotient Labelings from Edge Partitions
concept.concept_description: For any connected graph G with an edge partition P of E(G) into t classes, let A be the cycle-class parity matrix over GF(2) constructed from P. The induced quotient labeling ℓ: V(G) → (Z/2Z)^(t − rank(A)) satisfies d_G(u,v) ≥ d_H(ℓ(u), ℓ(v)) for all u,v ∈ V(G), where H is the hypercube Cayley graph on (Z/2Z)^(t − rank(A)). That is, the labeling never stretches distances—it can fail to be isometric only by shortcuts (contracting distances), never by stretching them.

The induced quotient labeling ℓ: V(G) → (Z/2Z)^(t − rank(A)) satisfies d_G(u,v) ≥ d_H(ℓ(u), ℓ(v)) for all u,v ∈ V(G), where H is the hypercube Cayley graph on (Z/2Z)^(t − rank(A)). concept.lean_guess: Show that each edge of G maps to an edge of H under the quotient labeling (by construction of the labeling from the edge partition), so every path in G maps to a path of equal or shorter length in H. The key step is proving that the GF(2) quotient construction preserves adjacency: if uv ∈ E(G) and uv lies in partition class i, then ℓ(u) and ℓ(v) differ in exactly the coordinate corresponding to the image of class i in the quotient. The non-stretching then follows by taking d_G(u,v) as the infimum over all path lengths, which bound the Hamming distance of the labels from below.
